beats.text: Bayes' theorem reverses a conditional probability by accounting for how common each group is. Imagine one hundred objects: twenty are type A and eighty are type B. A screening rule flags some objects from either group.

The rule flags ninety percent of type A and ten percent of type B. In this frequency model, that means eighteen flagged A objects and eight flagged B objects. The remaining objects are not part of the flagged comparison group.

Once a flag is observed, compare only the twenty-six flagged objects. Eighteen are type A, giving nine thirteenths, or about sixty-nine percent. The original ninety percent described flags within type A, not type A within flags.

Now make type A rarer: ten of a thousand objects, with the same flagging rates. There are nine flagged A objects and ninety-nine flagged B objects. The posterior falls to one twelfth, showing why base rates cannot be ignored.

practice.prompt: Type A accounts for 30% of objects. A rule flags 80% of A and 10% of non-A. Find P(A|flag) using frequencies out of 1,000.
practice.answer: There are 300 A, of which 240 are flagged, and 700 non-A, of which 70 are flagged. P(A|flag)=240/310=24/31≈0.7742.

practice.prompt: Repeat the calculation when A accounts for only 10%, the A flagging rate is 80%, and the non-A flagging rate is 20%.
practice.answer: Out of 1,000, 80 A and 180 non-A are flagged. P(A|flag)=80/260=4/13≈0.3077.

practice.prompt: Explain why '80% of A objects get flagged' does not by itself tell us the percentage of flagged objects that are A. Identify the missing information.
practice.answer: It describes P(flag|A), not P(A|flag). We also need the base rate P(A) and the flagging rate among non-A, which determine the full flagged group.

takeaway: To reverse a conditional probability, combine the relevant likelihoods with the base rates and normalize within the observed group.
scope: Bayes' theorem through a transparent frequency model and a base-rate change.
title: Bayes theorem
objective: Reverse a conditional probability using base rates and total probability.
